title: Co-RL: Unsupervised Reasoning from a Diverse Cohort
hook: Self-rewarding RL collapses because a model's errors reinforce themselves. Co-RL breaks the loop by having a diverse cohort of models grade each other — no labels at all.
key_points: RL for reasoning still leans on verifiable rewards, which get scarce as models pass what humans can check.
Self-rewarding RL removes the labels but reinforces the model's own biases, shrinking diversity until training collapses.
Co-RL trains several models that share no parameters, each rewarded by its peers' judgments.
Cohort diversity — different families, sizes, and rephrased samples — is the active ingredient: it decorrelates errors.
Reports +3.0–8.6% average gains on seven text benchmarks and +2.3–7.2% on four multimodal ones, with no ground truth.
content_html: Reinforcement learning has been the engine behind the reasoning jump in recent models, but its best results still depend on a verifier that knows the right answer. That's fine for math and code; it runs out exactly where you'd most want it — on problems past the point where humans can reliably judge. Self-rewarding RL is the obvious escape hatch, and it has a known failure mode: a model grading itself amplifies its own biases until responses homogenize and training collapses.
extra_html:
How it works

Co-RL replaces the single self-grader with a cohort. Multiple models, sharing no parameters, are optimized at the same time, each one's reward derived from its peers' judgments of its completions. The authors' central finding is that diversity is what makes this work: mixing model families, model sizes, and rephrased versions of the training samples reduces the correlated errors that let a feedback loop close on itself.

Why it matters

Across text-only and multimodal domains the authors report consistent gains over the base models and over prior label-free methods — average improvements of 3.0–8.6% on seven text benchmarks and 2.3–7.2% on four multimodal benchmarks — while matching or beating supervised methods without touching a single ground-truth label. It also preserves behavioral diversity rather than eroding it, which is the property self-rewarding RL loses first. Code is open-sourced.

related.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning
related.hook: DeepSeek shows strong reasoning can emerge from RL on verifiable rewards with minimal supervised data - and those reasoning traces can be distilled into smaller models.

related.title: LLM-as-a-Verifier: Verification as a New Scaling Axis
related.hook: Everyone scales pretraining, post-training, and test-time compute. This paper argues verification — checking if a solution is correct — is its own scaling axis, and hits SOTA on four agentic benchmarks.

flashcards.prompt: What goes wrong when a model trains purely on rewards derived from its own completions?
flashcards.back_html: Its existing biases get reinforced, response diversity shrinks, and outputs homogenize — a self-reinforcing feedback loop that can end in training collapse.

flashcards.prompt: In Co-RL, where does the reward signal come from?

choices.text: From peer models in the cohort, which share no parameters
From a verifier that checks answers against ground-truth labels
From a single frozen reward model trained on human preferences

flashcards.explanation_html: Co-RL optimizes several decoupled models simultaneously, each scored by the others. No ground-truth labels are used.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the paper push for heterogeneous model families and sizes in the cohort?

choices.text: Diversity reduces correlated errors, which is what drives self-reinforcing collapse
Larger models need smaller ones to distill into during training
It lets the cohort be sharded across cheaper hardware

flashcards.explanation_html: If every peer makes the same mistake, peer reward is no better than self-reward. Decorrelating errors is what makes the mutual signal informative.
